clue.text: Xylophone and minute bass used in Sound Of Music song

indicators.note: the two letters are put to use inside the song title, so they go within it

parts.note: Maria is a song from the musical The Sound of Music
B is the abbreviation for bass in music

explanation.surface: Instruments and a deep voice part being worked into a number from a famous musical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'used in' puts M and B inside MARIA, between its I and final A.
explanation.definitionFit: A marimba is a large African-origin percussion instrument of the xylophone family, with wooden bars and resonators.

clue.text: Harmful fellow having officer stripped?

parts.note: a fellow is a man, a male

indicators.note: the word officer is stripped of its two outer layers on each side, leaving only its core

explanation.surface: A nasty man who has had an officer stripped of rank or clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stripped' peels OF and ER off the two ends of OFFICER, leaving FIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Malefic is a literary word for causing harm or evil, a direct synonym of harmful.

clue.text: Master in business initially game for a dance

parts.note: RU is rugby union, a game
M is the abbreviation for Master, as in a degree

indicators.note: only the first letter of the word business is wanted

explanation.surface: An MBA graduate is up for joining in a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like an MBA (Master in Business Administration) but supplies M and B separately; RU, the game, goes in front despite coming later in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The rumba is a ballroom and Latin dance of Cuban origin.

clue.text: Greeting early in the day is heard

indicators.note: the word meant by early in the day is spoken, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: the early part of the day is the morning

explanation.surface: A 'good morning' greeting being heard at the start of the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greeting' looks like a salutation, but it is the Scots sense of weeping, lamenting.
explanation.definitionFit: Greeting in its Scottish sense means weeping or lamenting, which is grieving for the dead.

clue.text: A child regularly rejected tart

indicators.note: every other letter of child is thrown out at regular intervals, keeping the 1st, 3rd and 5th

explanation.surface: A youngster keeps turning down a pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly rejected' drops H and L from CHILD, leaving CID; 'tart' is the sharp-tasting adjective, not the pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: Acid as an adjective means sour or sharp to taste, a synonym of tart.

clue.text: Section of road unexpectedly usable around noon

indicators.note: the rearranged letters sit around the abbreviation for noon
the letters of usable come out in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: A stretch of road surprisingly passable at midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unexpectedly' rearranges USABLE to BUSLAE, and 'around' wraps that round N.
explanation.definitionFit: A bus lane is a strip of carriageway reserved for buses, so a part of the road.

clue.text: Complaint about nosh served up, fast food

parts.note: a beef is slang for a grievance or complaint

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means the pieces are written upwards, back to front

parts.note: RE is a Latin-derived word for about, concerning
nosh and grub are both slang for food

explanation.surface: A grumble about the food that gets dished out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'served up' turns RE + GRUB into BURGER.
explanation.definitionFit: A beefburger is a minced-meat patty in a bun, a staple of takeaway catering.

clue.text: Position of lectern lacking base at front of church

indicators.note: the shortened stand goes in front of the church abbreviation
in a down clue the base is the bottom letter, which is dropped

parts.note: a lectern is a reading stand
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Where the lectern stands, without its base, at the front of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacking base' drops the final D of STAND, leaving STAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A stance is a stated position or attitude on an issue, or a way of standing.

clue.text: Little time, say, to enter roughly half the clues in word puzzles

indicators.note: the soundalike enters the other piece, going inside it

parts.note: in a crossword roughly half the clues are the across ones

indicators.note: say asks for a word spoken alike, the tic that sounds like tick

parts.note: a tick is a moment, a little time

explanation.surface: Puzzle-setter taking a moment to slip something into half the clues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' marks a soundalike: the little time is a tick, written the way a nervous twitch is spelt.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrostics are word puzzles in which initial or other letters of lines spell out words.

clue.text: Musician stimulated Norsemen no end

indicators.note: stimulated suggests stirred up, so the remaining letters are shaken into a new order
the word Norsemen loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A musician who got Vikings worked up endlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end' leaves NORSEME, which 'stimulated' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Keith Emerson was a rock keyboard player, of Emerson, Lake and Palmer.

clue.text: Old American at home in green luxury vehicle

indicators.note: the three short pieces go inside the colour

parts.note: lime is a shade of green
US means American
in means at home

explanation.surface: An elderly American at home in a smart green car.
explanation.definitionFit: A limousine is a large chauffeur-driven car, the classic luxury vehicle.

clue.text: Half of Reds in time for match

indicators.note: the half word goes inside the period of time

parts.note: an age is a period of time

indicators.note: only the first half of the four-letter word Reds is used

explanation.surface: Half the Reds team turning up in time for the game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'match' looks like the game in the surface, but it is a verb meaning correspond.
explanation.definitionFit: To agree is to correspond or tally, as two accounts or descriptions match.

clue.text: Relative joins floor show ostentatiously

indicators.note: the relative joins on after the floor abbreviation

parts.note: an aunt is a relative

explanation.surface: A family member takes to the dance floor to show off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'show' looks like a noun after 'floor', but it is a verb in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To flaunt something is to display it conspicuously, showing off.

clue.text: Jack charges only one cent for outdated calculators

parts.note: a jack is a sailor, abbreviated AB (able seaman)

indicators.note: of the two cent letters in the word for charges, only one is kept

parts.note: to charge is to accuse

explanation.surface: A man called Jack charging just one cent for old adding machines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'only one' keeps one of the two Cs of ACCUSES, giving ACUSES.
explanation.definitionFit: Abacuses are bead-frame counting devices, superseded by electronic calculators.

clue.text: Guess I'm stuck in English railway terminal

indicators.note: the first person words get wedged inside the railway building

parts.note: a terminal on the railway is a station

explanation.surface: Someone guessing that they are stranded at an English railway terminus.
explanation.definitionFit: An estimation is a rough calculation or judgement, a guess at a value.

clue.text: A number taped by Culture Club maybe repulsed the Mafia

indicators.note: the inserted piece is held inside, as though taped up by the other
repulsed means driven back, so the society is written backwards

parts.note: an arts society, ARTS SOC, is an example of a club for culture

explanation.surface: A song recorded by the pop band Culture Club, rejected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Culture Club' is not the band but an arts society, ARTS SOC; 'repulsed' gives COSSTRA, and 'taped by' puts ANO inside after COS.
explanation.definitionFit: Cosa Nostra, Italian for 'our thing', is a name for the Sicilian and American Mafia.

clue.text: Woman crosses Loire zigzagging towards northern coast

indicators.note: the woman stretches across the other letters, placing them inside

parts.note: she refers to a woman

indicators.note: the river's letters zigzag into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman crossing the River Loire, winding her way towards the northern coast.
explanation.walkthrough: The Loire is a French river; only its letters matter here.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoreline is the line where land meets the sea, the coast.

clue.text: Female encounters local inhabitant of Helsinki?

indicators.note: the female letter meets up with the pub, sitting next to it

parts.note: a local is a pub near home, an inn

explanation.surface: A woman bumping into a local resident in the Finnish capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'local' is the British word for a neighbourhood pub, not a resident. The question mark flags that a Finn is only one example of a Helsinki dweller.
explanation.definitionFit: A Finn is a native of Finland, whose capital is Helsinki.

clue.text: Cheeky swimmer from Portsmouth found here?

definitions.meaning: a swimmer setting off from Portsmouth would be in the Solent, the strait between the city and the Isle of Wight

explanation.surface: A rude swimmer setting off from the naval city of Portsmouth.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the second reading after two letters: a swimmer leaving Portsmouth, a naval port on England's south coast, is in the waters of the Solent.
explanation.definitionFit: Insolent means rudely disrespectful, the same as impudent or cheeky.

clue.text: Husband having love affair over in vicinity of the Bronx?

parts.note: love in tennis is zero, the letter O

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the party word goes backwards

parts.note: a do is a party or social affair

explanation.surface: A husband carrying on an affair somewhere in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affair' is a party, DO, not a romance; 'over' turns it to OD.
explanation.definitionFit: Hood is American slang for neighbourhood, as in a district of the Bronx in New York.

clue.text: Prisoner that almost goes off the rails

indicators.note: out of control, so the letters are thrown into disorder
the word that loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A prisoner who is nearly going out of control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims THAT to THA; 'off the rails' rearranges THA plus GOES.
explanation.definitionFit: A hostage is a person held captive as security for demands, a prisoner.

clue.text: Don't say I've reviewed unpleasant film

indicators.note: reviewed suggests looked at again, with the letters seen in a new order

explanation.surface: A critic refusing to admit they have reviewed a nasty movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reviewed' rearranges the letters of DON'T SAY I'VE; the apostrophes are ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: Video nasty was the 1980s British term for a violent or gory horror film on tape.

clue.text: Old Russian leader's desire to suppress Leninist extremists is backfiring

indicators.note: the longing holds down the other letters inside it

parts.note: a yen is a longing or desire

indicators.note: only the two end letters of the word Leninist are used
backfiring sends the word is the wrong way, back to front

explanation.surface: A former Kremlin chief's wish to crush Leninist hardliners goes wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremists' looks like political hardliners, but it asks only for the end letters of Leninist.
explanation.definitionFit: Boris Yeltsin was the first president of the Russian Federation, from 1991 to 1999.

clue.text: Bird left in nest first to soar away

indicators.note: away signals that this letter is taken out of the word nest
the first letter of the word soar is what goes

explanation.surface: A bird quitting its nest and soaring off for the first time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first to soar' is S, and 'away' takes it out of NEST, leaving NET.
explanation.definitionFit: The linnet is a small brown finch common in Britain and Europe.

clue.text: Novel delivered by a northern writer once

parts.note: She is a novel by H Rider Haggard
rid as in delivered from, freed

explanation.surface: A book handed over by a writer from the north of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like an adjective but is the title SHE.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Brinsley Sheridan was an 18th-century Irish playwright, author of The Rivals.

clue.text: Wartime commander from Melbourne held prisoner

indicators.note: the letters are held captive inside the words from Melbourne

explanation.surface: A military chief from an Australian city taken captive in the war.
explanation.definitionFit: Erwin Rommel was a German field marshal of the Second World War, the Desert Fox.

clue.text: A thousand and two old articles rot!

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

indicators.note: two calls for the old article twice

parts.note: ye is an old form of the definite article

explanation.surface: A thousand and two antique items decaying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rot' is the exclamation of disbelief, not decay.
explanation.definitionFit: 'My eye!' is an old-fashioned exclamation meaning nonsense, just as 'Rot!' dismisses something.

clue.text: Ms Streisand's no artist? An unkind thing to say!

indicators.note: no means without, so the artist is taken away

parts.note: Barbra Streisand, the American singer and actor
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: A cutting claim that Barbra Streisand is no artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no' removes RA from BARBRA, leaving BARB.
explanation.definitionFit: A barb is a cutting, hurtful remark, like the hook on an arrow.

clue.text: Sci-fi film once considered more suitable for adults? Right

parts.words: once considered more suitable for adults
parts.note: A was the former British film certificate for films more suitable for adults
a lien is a legal right to hold property until a debt is paid

explanation.surface: A science-fiction movie once rated as adult viewing, and rightly so.
explanation.walkthrough: A was a British film rating used before 1982 for films judged more suitable for adults.
explanation.definitionFit: Alien is Ridley Scott's 1979 science-fiction horror film.

clue.text: Anger as I speed towards headland

parts.note: a rate is a speed
ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness or Dungeness

explanation.surface: Fury as someone races towards a promontory.
explanation.definitionFit: Irateness is the state of being irate, that is fury or wrath.

clue.text: Female tennis champ formerly on team

parts.note: Chris Evert, US tennis champion of the 1970s and 1980s

explanation.surface: A former women's tennis champion joining a side.
explanation.walkthrough: Everton is an English Premier League football club from Liverpool.
explanation.definitionFit: Everton is a football club, so a team in the sporting sense.

clue.text: Marsh bird — part sea bird

parts.note: a bit is a part or piece
a tern is a sea bird

explanation.surface: A wetland bird that is partly a seabird.
explanation.definitionFit: The bittern is a heron-like wading bird of reedbeds, famous for its booming call.
